title: Starting a Hospice in North Carolina: Licensing, Costs, and Step-by-Step Guide

Introduction (2-3 paragraphs)

Starting a Hospice in North Carolina represents a meaningful opportunity to serve terminally ill patients and their families while building a compliant, sustainable care business. Oversight and funding are administered by the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services (NC DHHS), Division of Health Service Regulation (DHSR), which handles all state-level licensing and inspections. For providers seeking to serve the majority of the eligible population, reimbursement and program funding are coordinated through the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).

With strong market signals including consistent demand that exceeds provider capacity and a recent $1.8 million state investment in pediatric hospice, North Carolina offers a favorable market with significant growth opportunities, particularly in underserved rural regions. Providers can expect reimbursement rates for routine home care to be in the $190-$250 per day range, creating a viable financial model for those prepared to navigate the state’s rigorous licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements.

This comprehensive guide walks you through every step of launching a Hospice in North Carolina, from understanding complex regulations and obtaining a Certificate of Need (CoN) to staffing your interdisciplinary team, managing reimbursement, and preparing for state and federal inspections.

  • Understand North Carolina’s Hospice Regulations

Section 1: Understand North Carolina’s Hospice Regulations

North Carolina regulates Hospice programs through the NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation (DHSR), which is responsible for issuing licenses, conducting inspections, and enforcing state rules to ensure patient safety and quality of care. The primary state-level rules are outlined in 10A NCAC 13K and 13J. A critical and often challenging prerequisite in North Carolina is the requirement to obtain a Certificate of Need (CoN) before a license can be granted, which demonstrates a public need for the new service in a specific geographic area.

Providers serving Medicare or Medicaid populations, which constitute the vast majority of hospice patients, must also comply with federal frameworks established by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). These federal regulations, known as the Hospice Conditions of Participation (CoPs), govern everything from patient rights and care planning to quality reporting and billing. The state and federal regulatory framework emphasizes a patient-centered approach focused on compassionate palliative care, symptom management, and support for the patient and their family. Licenses are issued by DHSR and typically require renewal every 1 year.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

While all licensed hospices provide a core set of services, North Carolina’s market supports multiple specialized program models, each with different operational focuses and opportunities:

  • Pediatric Hospice: A high-demand niche focused on providing specialized palliative and end-of-life care for children and their families. The state’s recent $1.8 million investment highlights the recognized need in this area.
  • Rural Service Provision: Targeting underserved rural counties where access to hospice care is limited. While logistically challenging, this model addresses a critical gap and may face less competition.
  • Integrated Home Health/Hospice Models: Offering a continuum of care that allows patients to transition seamlessly from curative home health services to palliative hospice care with the same trusted provider.
  • Academic Medical Center Collaborations: Partnering with large hospitals and health systems to serve as their preferred hospice provider, ensuring a steady stream of referrals and close clinical integration.

Program size in North Carolina can vary significantly, ranging from small, community-based programs with a modest patient census to larger, multi-county agencies serving hundreds of patients. Demand is strongest and most visible in urban centers, but the greatest unmet need and opportunity for new providers is in rural counties, which often have significant access disparities. These lower-penetration regions may offer a clearer path through the Certificate of Need process and a chance to establish a vital community resource with less direct competition.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Before you can provide care, you must establish a formal business entity and navigate a multi-phase licensing process. Providers typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC) or S-Corporation to create a legal separation between the business and its owners. The foundational steps include:

  • Register your business with the North Carolina Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS for tax purposes.
  • Secure required insurance, including general liability and professional liability (malpractice) coverage.
  • Obtain a Certificate of Need (CoN) from the Healthcare Planning and Certificate of Need Section of DHHS. This is a mandatory, data-driven process and the most significant barrier to entry.
  • Submit a licensing application to the DHSR once the CoN is approved.

Licensing timelines in North Carolina are extensive and can take up to 6 months or longer, largely dependent on the CoN process and the completeness of your application. The DHSR process is typically broken into three phases:

  • Phase 1: Prerequisites (up to 3 months): This includes securing your CoN, developing policies, and preparing all required documentation.
  • Phase 2: Submission (up to 60 days): The period during which you submit your complete application packet to DHSR for initial review.
  • Phase 3: Review and Inspection (up to 120 days): DHSR conducts a thorough review, followed by an initial licensure survey of your office and operations before a license is issued.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is essential for securing funding and guiding your launch. Startup costs for a hospice in North Carolina typically range from $75,000 to $250,000, depending on factors like office lease costs, initial staffing, technology (EMR systems), and legal fees associated with the CoN and licensure process.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by your clinical and administrative team, with staffing representing approximately 60-70% of total costs. Your revenue will be determined by reimbursement rates from Medicare, Medicaid, and private insurers. A typical revenue snapshot includes:

  • Routine Home Care (RHC): $190 – $250 per patient per day
  • Continuous Home Care (CHC): Reimbursed on an hourly basis for crisis care
  • Inpatient Respite Care: $300+ per day
  • General Inpatient Care (GIP): The highest daily rate for managing complex symptoms in a facility setting.

With a strong referral network and efficient operations, providers operating at a target census of 80% of their projected capacity can generally achieve healthy 10-15% profit margins. Most new hospices can expect to reach a break-even point within 6 to 12 months of becoming fully operational and Medicare-certified.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

Unlike residential facilities, a hospice agency’s primary physical location is its administrative office. However, this office must meet specific state and federal requirements to ensure compliance. Your facility must adhere to the following:

  • A physical administrative office that is accessible to staff and the public during business hours.
  • Secure, locked storage for patient records and other confidential information to comply with HIPAA.
  • Compliance with local zoning ordinances and building codes for a business or medical office.
  • Sufficient space for your interdisciplinary team meetings, administrative staff, and supply storage.
  • If you plan to offer General Inpatient (GIP) care, you must either contract with a licensed hospital or skilled nursing facility or build out a dedicated, licensed inpatient hospice unit that meets much stricter healthcare facility construction standards.

When selecting a location, consider its proximity to major referral sources like hospitals, its accessibility for your staff who will be traveling throughout the service area, and the availability of a qualified clinical workforce in the vicinity.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Your interdisciplinary team is the heart of your hospice. North Carolina regulations and CMS Conditions of Participation mandate specific roles and qualifications. Required roles for your team typically include:

  • Hospice Director/Administrator: Responsible for overall agency management. A Bachelor’s degree is preferred, with at least 2+ years of relevant healthcare management experience.
  • Medical Director: A physician who provides clinical oversight and certifies patient eligibility.
  • Registered Nurse (RN) Case Managers: An RN must be continuously available (on-call) 24/7. RNs lead care planning and direct patient services.
  • Direct Care Staff (CNAs/Aides): Must be at least 18 years old and complete required training.
  • Social Workers (MSW)
  • Spiritual Counselors/Chaplains
  • Bereavement Counselors

Training is a major focus of regulatory oversight. All direct care staff must complete 12 hours of initial orientation training before providing patient care, followed by 12 hours of annual continuing education. All licensed professionals (RNs, LPNs, MSWs) must maintain their licenses in good standing and meet their respective board’s continuing education requirements.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Your operational guidebook is your set of policies and procedures. North Carolina’s DHSR and CMS will not issue a license without a comprehensive, customized set of policies that govern every aspect of your agency. State rules require written policies covering:

  • Patient Rights and Responsibilities
  • Admission, Transfer, and Discharge Criteria
  • Development and Review of the Plan of Care
  • Pain and Symptom Management Protocols
  • Medication Management and Administration
  • Emergency Procedures and On-Call Protocols
  • Staffing Plans, Training, and Supervision
  • Infection Control
  • Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI)

Central to hospice operations is the individualized plan of care. This document must be developed by the full interdisciplinary team in collaboration with the patient and family within days of admission. It must be reviewed and updated regularly (typically every 15 days) to reflect the patient’s changing needs and goals. Meticulous documentation of these plans and team meetings is a primary focus of all regulatory surveys.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Unlike many consumer-facing businesses, hospice marketing is not about public advertising. Success depends on building strong, trust-based relationships with professional referral sources. Your marketing efforts should be entirely focused on business-to-business development. Referrals for hospice care in North Carolina typically come from:

  • Hospital discharge planners and case managers
  • Oncologists and other physician specialists
  • Primary care physicians
  • Skilled nursing facility (SNF) administrators and directors of nursing
  • Assisted living community directors
  • Home health agencies

Successful providers establish themselves as reliable, responsive, and compliant partners. Your reputation for excellent clinical care, clear communication, and positive patient outcomes will be your most powerful marketing tool. Focus on demonstrating your value to physicians and facility managers who are entrusting their patients to your care.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Oversight in hospice is continuous. Your agency will be subject to regular and unannounced inspections from surveying bodies including the NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation (DHSR) for state licensure and CMS (or its accrediting-body contractors) for Medicare certification.

Inspectors focus heavily on documentation and direct observation to ensure you are meeting the standards of care. Some of the most common deficiencies found during hospice surveys include:

  • Incomplete or outdated patient plans of care.
  • Insufficient documentation of interdisciplinary team meetings and care coordination.
  • Errors in medication management or reconciliation.
  • Lack of documentation proving required staff training and competency.
  • Failure to provide services (e.g., social work, spiritual care) as outlined in the plan of care.

To succeed, you must foster a culture of continuous quality improvement (QAPI) and maintain audit-ready documentation at all times. Regularly conduct self-audits of your patient charts and internal processes to identify and correct potential issues before a surveyor finds them.

Conclusion

Starting a Hospice in North Carolina is a complex but deeply rewarding venture. The state’s growing demand, particularly in rural areas, presents a clear opportunity for new providers dedicated to compassionate end-of-life care. Success requires careful planning, a deep understanding of the regulatory landscape—especially the Certificate of Need process—and unwavering operational discipline. Providers who invest in compliance, build a strong interdisciplinary team, and cultivate professional referral relationships are positioned for long-term success and community impact.
